name: 加登長 横安江町店 (Kadochō Yokoanjemachi-ten)

claims.text: Wheat udon and soba share kitchen and likely boiling water; fried items (tempura, katsu) use wheat batter/breading. No allergen separation is documented.
Standard Japanese soy-sauce-and-dashi broths are used throughout; conventional soy sauce contains wheat.
Broths rely on fish/bonito dashi and the menu centers on fish, egg, and meat dishes; no vegan preparation is indicated.

name: 加賀麸司 宮田・鈴庵 (Kaga Fuzukasa Miyata Suzuan)

claims.text: The restaurant's core ingredient, fu, is wheat gluten; virtually every dish on the fu courses is wheat-based, so the entire menu is unsafe for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.
Traditional Kaga preparations such as jibuni rely on Japanese soy sauce and broth, which standardly contain wheat; no wheat-free seasoning is documented.

Courses include jibuni (chicken/duck and dashi) and egg dishes, and dashi-based seasoning is used across the menu, so plant-only fu dishes are not guaranteed and would need to be requested in advance.

name: 加賀料理 大名茶家 (Kaga Ryori Daimyo Chaya)

claims.text: No gluten-free handling or dedicated equipment is documented; the cuisine is soy-sauce- and dashi-based, so cross-contamination with wheat should be assumed.
Traditional Kaga dishes such as jibuni and simmered/grilled preparations use Japanese soy sauce and tare, which normally contain wheat.
A seafood- and dashi-centered kaiseki kitchen; no separate vegan preparation is documented, so animal-derived broth and cross-contact should be expected.

name: 加賀料理 魚半 (Kaga Ryori Gyohan)

claims.text: Signature jibu-ni/jibu-nabe is dusted/thickened with wheat flour and simmered in a soy-sauce-and-dashi broth, and nama-fu (wheat gluten) dengaku is a menu item, so gluten is central to the kitchen; deep-fried gori and tempura mean shared frying oil is likely.
Dishes rely on standard Japanese soy sauce and dashi-based seasonings, which contain wheat; no gluten-free soy sauce or protocol is documented.

Menu is centered on duck, local fish (gori, nodoguro, sweet shrimp), and crab, with broths built on seafood/katsuo dashi, so animal-derived ingredients are pervasive and no vegan preparation is documented.

name: 海鮮市場料理 市の蔵 (Kaisen Ichiba Ryori Ichi no Kura)

claims.text: Cuisine is built on soy sauce, miso, and dashi (jibuni stew, grilled dishes, set meals), which in standard Japanese cooking contain or involve wheat; no gluten-free alternatives are documented.
A seafood- and meat-centered kitchen using fish dashi throughout; no vegan or vegetarian preparation is mentioned.

name: 海鮮酒処 あげは (Kaisen Sakedokoro Ageha)

claims.text: Surimi/satsuma-age (fried fish paste) and seafood manju are the core dishes; fish-paste products and fried items typically contain wheat, and no gluten-free handling is documented.
Sashimi is served as part of the set, normally eaten with soy sauce, which in Japan generally contains wheat.
The entire menu is built around fish, seafood, and fish paste; no plant-based dishes are documented.

name: 海鮮丼ひかりや 近江町市場店 (Kaisendon Hikariya Omicho Ichiba-ten)

claims.text: Bowls are seasoned with a house sesame-soy sauce (特製ごま醤油だれ) and finished by pouring hot dashi to make chazuke; standard soy sauce and dashi typically contain wheat, making the dish unsafe for celiacs.
Menu is entirely raw fish and shellfish bowls (ikura, crab, shrimp, tuna, octopus, scallop) over rice with fish-based dashi; no plant-based options documented.
Raw fish over rice is served with standard wheat-based soy sauce; no gluten-free accommodation is documented.
As a sashimi/donburi shop, standard Japanese soy sauce (which contains wheat) is the default condiment.
Every documented dish is seafood-based; raw fish is the core ingredient, so vegan cross-contact is unavoidable.
